title: The mirror in the mind
text: Watch someone yawn and you will probably yawn too; laughter, smiling and a colleague's nervous foot-tapping spread through groups in the same way. Behavioural scientists call the tendency the chameleon effect, a species of unconscious {{1}} (MIMIC) that makes moods, like yawns, quietly {{2}} (CONTAGION). In the 1990s the phenomenon acquired a possible mechanism. Recording single cells in monkeys' brains, researchers in Parma found neurons that fired both when an animal grasped a peanut and — {{3}} (ASTONISH) — when it merely watched a human grasp one. These so-called mirror neurons launched a thousand {{4}} (SPECULATE): perhaps they underpin empathy, language, even culture itself. The subsequent decades were more sobering. Attempts to find clean mirror systems in humans produced a {{5}} (CONFUSE) picture, and the grander claims have not survived. The present consensus is {{6}} (CONSIDER) humbler: imitation is real and important, but it is one system among several. What is not in doubt is imitation's reach. Newborns copy facial expressions within hours of birth, children acquire skills chiefly by copying, and adults continue to adopt the posture, accent and vocabulary of their company — the engine of {{7}} (CULTURE) transmission, by which accents, dances and customs travel between generations. Whatever the cellular truth, the practical lesson is old and {{8}} (OBSERVE): spend a dinner with your arms crossed, and watch the table slowly follow.

gaps.explanation: 'moods are quietly contagious' — the adjective of this family is contagious.
'and — astonishingly — when it watched' — adverb from astonish.
'launched a thousand speculations' — plural pinned by 'a thousand'.
'a confusing picture' — the results cause confusion.
'old and observable' — able to be observed, from observe.
